title: Implement lightweight SDK request-propagation adapter and runtime hook
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: We currently have multiple ad-hoc mechanisms for carrying request context (trace ids, customer metadata) across internal services and SDKs. This causes loss of continuity in traces for legacy clients and inconsistent sampling metadata in the console dashboards. Goal: Deliver a small, low-latency SDK adapter and a runtime hook that ensures robust context propagation for sync and async flows while minimizing per-request overhead. The adapter must support W3C traceparent/tracestate, a lightweight 'x-rd-ctx' extension header for legacy clients, and an opt-in automatic instrumentation mode for frameworks that support middleware hooks.
acceptance_criteria: SDK adapter exposes a single API: attachContext(ctx) / extractContext(headers) usable in node/python/java SDKs (POC for node).
Runtime hook attaches and forwards context for both sync and fiber/async task execution paths with <1% p99 latency regression in our synthetic benchmark.
Header compatibility: fully parse and propagate W3C traceparent + tracestate and a documented Redwood extension header without dropping existing headers.
End-to-end traces in staging demonstrate preserved parent/child relationships across HTTP/gRPC boundaries with both legacy and instrumented clients.
Console dashboards show improved trace coverage for the sampled test traffic; new dashboard tiles for context-loss rate and header-parse failures are created.
Security review sign-off for the extension header and any KMS-related fields if present.
notes: Spike completed (2025-02-21): implemented node shim that adds a 2ms median overhead for cold requests and <1% CPU increase under our benchmark load.
Decision: We will support two modes: manual (explicit attach/extract) and automatic middleware-enabled propagation. Automatic mode is opt-in at SDK init to avoid surprising customers.

Trade-off: Redwood extension header (x-rd-ctx) carries small internal metadata but is not encrypted. Any sensitive customer fields must be stored in our request store and referenced by a short opaque id instead.

Implementation approach: Create a tiny header parser in core runtime to avoid repeated allocations, and expose safe language-level adapters in SDKs that share a canonical binary encoding scheme (base64-compact) documented in the design doc.
Rollout plan: Canary in staging -> 5% of internal traffic -> gradual ramp to 50% with rollback window. Add automated regression checks for p95/p99 latency and memory allocation.
implementation_plan: Week 1: Finalize header schema and implement core header parser in runtime (C++/Rust path).
Week 2: Ship Node SDK adapter and middleware shim; add comprehensive unit tests for header edge cases.
Week 3: Integrate runtime hook for async fibers and worker pools; run load benchmarks and tune allocation paths.
Week 4: Create console dashboard tiles (context-loss rate, header-parse-failures) and alerting rules; perform security review and docs.
Week 5: Canary release + monitor; collect metrics and rollout or rollback based on SLOs.
risks: Header bloat: adding too much data to propagated headers can increase network and CPU cost; we cap extension size to 256 bytes.
Backward compatibility: legacy clients might send non-standard encodings; the parser must be defensive and emit parse-failure metrics rather than crashing.
Performance regressions on hot paths: need microbenchmarks to ensure p99 latency targets are maintained.
Security: accidental propagation of sensitive customer metadata if SDKs misuse extension fields; require secure coding checklist and security review.
